chunks: DMM sample rate and whether it matters. The question: What is a DMM's sample rate? Does it matter?
A multimeter does not watch the signal continuously the way a scope does. It averages the input over a short window, then shows one number.
"Sample rate" really means readings per second.
The averaging window is what makes a multimeter accurate and quiet on a steady signal, and what makes it blind to anything that changes quickly.
Think of a long-exposure photograph. A still building comes out sharp. Cars driving past blur into nothing, or vanish. A multimeter's reading is like that long exposure.
A steady battery voltage is the building, and a brief glitch is a car that drives through during the exposure.
Longer exposures give cleaner pictures of still things but erase more motion.
noise falls with the square root of integration time until a floor from 1/f noise and thermal EMFs takes over. Beyond about 10 to 100 NPLC, extra time buys little.
The floor level here is illustrative.
Reading rate: how many readings per second the meter shows. Integration time: how long the meter averages the input for each reading.
Mains hum: pickup at the power-line frequency, 50 or 60 hertz. NPLC: number of power-line cycles in the averaging window. 1 NPLC at 60 hertz is 1 over 60 seconds equals 16.
7 milliseconds. Aliasing: a fast variation looking like a slow one because readings come too rarely.
Set a meter to 1 NPLC on 60 hertz mains. Each reading averages for 16. 7 milliseconds, so the top speed is about 60 readings a second.
Averaging over a whole number of mains cycles also cancels 60 hertz hum, because a sine wave averages to zero over a full cycle. Averaging longer cuts random noise too.
For a steady 3. 3 volts rail, slow is better. But say the rail dips by 1 volts for 1 milliseconds and resets a processor.
Averaged over a slow 100 milliseconds window, that dip moves the reading by only about 10 millivolts. The meter shows a calm 3. 30 volts while the processor resets.
That is the whole idea.
"A DMM's sample rate is really readings per second, set by how long it integrates, usually a number of power-line cycles. At 1 NPLC on 60 hertz that's about 16.
7 milliseconds, so up to ~60 readings a second; handhelds give a few per second.
Longer integration gives lower noise, roughly one over root-time, and better 50/60 hertz rejection.
It matters for anything that changes within a reading: glitches, ripple, transients get averaged away or even alias. For a steady DC rail it doesn't matter, and slower is better."
